profile.title: Fragile Action-Stage Dietary Change in a Pregnant Woman with Prediabetes and Prior Second-Trimester Loss
profile.summary: This case teaches dietetics students to conduct a telehealth nutrition assessment with a chatty, high-health-literacy pregnant patient whose fragile action-stage dietary changes and food-insecurity-driven eating pattern require patient-centered, non-judgmental elicitation. The core teaching points are managing a circumstantial communication style to extract a complete diet history, uncovering a self-report-versus-OB-chart mismatch around prenatal vitamin adherence without shaming the patient, and building a realistic, budget- and pantry-compatible meal plan for a household of eight while reinforcing recently started, still-shaky positive changes.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Union, New Jersey, seated in her kitchen with household noise audible in the background

patient.name: Velda Schuster
patient.occupation: Part-time receptionist at a dental office
patient.appearance: Appears tired but animated, with dark circles under her eyes; sits with legs crossed/elevated for comfort due to mild ankle swelling; lips slightly dry; gestures a lot while talking, phone and a sales flyer visible nearby, occasional background noise from kids in the house

persona.personality: Warm, talkative, eager to be liked and seen as competent and capable; uses humor to soften hard topics; proud and private about struggles, especially around asking for help
persona.communicationStyle: Tells long, winding stories that start on topic, drift into family anecdotes or things she read online, and loop back around to answer the original question; speaks quickly, gestures a lot, loses her thread mid-sentence then circles back; responds well to gentle, patient redirection and isn't offended by it
persona.emotionalState: Generally upbeat and animated on the surface, but tired and running on fragmented sleep; becomes quieter and more guarded when conversation nears the 2023 miscarriage or her vitamin lapses, tearing up briefly if pressed gently on the vitamin gap
persona.background: Velda grew up in Union, New Jersey in a big extended family where meals always stretched to feed whoever showed up, and she's carried that instinct into her own household of eight. She works part-time as a dental receptionist, is married, and considers herself the one everyone leans on. She shops with sales flyers, times trips to her favorite ShopRite for markdown produce, keeps a running list of 'good food swaps' on her phone from things she's read online, and talks to her sister two towns over most days by phone even though her sister can't help in person day-to-day.
speechExamples: Oh honey, let me tell you about my morning - actually wait, you asked about breakfast, right? Okay so breakfast...
I read this thing online, hold on, lemme find it - no actually I remember it, it said oats are a 'slow carb' so I figured I was doing good
I'm fine, I'm always fine, that's kind of my whole deal, ha - but go ahead, ask me whatever you need to ask
Sorry, sorry, I do that, I go on and on - ask me again, I promise I'll actually answer this time
It's not that big a deal, I just... some days I forget, that's all, everybody forgets sometimes right?
concerns: That her prediabetes will turn into something worse after this baby comes
That she's not resting enough to keep her blood pressure where it should be
That she won't be able to keep up the changes she just started once life gets busy again
Whether the vegetables and food at the pantry are 'good enough' to actually help her and the baby

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition follow-up visit with Velda Schuster, a 31-year-old woman who is currently pregnant and has had prediabetes since 2017. She was referred for diet counseling during this pregnancy. Review her available health record before the call. Your job today is to complete a nutrition assessment, identify a nutrition diagnosis, and provide patient-centered counseling and education for the remainder of this visit.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Nutrition follow-up visit for diet counseling during pregnancy with a history of prediabetes
scenario.openingLine: Hi! Thanks for fitting me in, it's a little loud over here, my youngest is having a whole opera in the next room, ha - but yeah, I'm here! The doctor's office said y'all wanted to check in on how I'm eating now that I'm pregnant again, so, here I am.
tasks: Take a focused diet and lifestyle history, including meal pattern, household food resources, and recent changes she's made
Review relevant anthropometric and laboratory data to inform your nutrition assessment
Identify barriers to consistent healthy eating and supplement adherence in her daily life
Formulate a nutrition diagnosis and realistic, budget-appropriate plan tailored to her household and resources
Reinforce her recent dietary changes using patient-centered counseling techniques

artifacts.title: OB Visit Note - 2026-08-21
artifacts.author: Obstetrics, Union Family Health
artifacts.body:
31-year-old G_P_ at approximately 20 weeks gestation presenting for fetal anatomy ultrasound and antenatal alpha-fetoprotein screening. Fetal anatomy survey unremarkable; AFP sent, pending at time of visit.

Interval history: Patient reports ongoing nausea, improved compared to first trimester but still present intermittently. On medication reconciliation, patient reports she went approximately one full week without taking her prenatal vitamin in early August 2026 due to nausea when taking it, then resumed. Counseled on taking prenatal vitamin with food or at bedtime to reduce nausea. Patient verbalized understanding.

No vaginal bleeding, no cramping, fetal movement reportedly present. Discussed warning signs to call for. Follow-up scheduled.

objectives.text: Elicit a complete diet and lifestyle history despite a circumstantial, story-driven communication style, capturing household meal patterns, food access strategies, and self-sacrificing eating behaviors.

Integrate anthropometric and laboratory data (BMI, weight trend, HbA1c, fasting glucose, lipids) into a nutrition assessment, correctly distinguishing relevant findings from historical data that predates the current pregnancy.
Explore prenatal vitamin and supplement adherence in a non-judgmental way, identifying the gap between what the patient reports and what the chart documents.
Identify psychosocial and household barriers—including minimal practical support, food insecurity/pantry use, and inconsistent work hours—that affect her ability to sustain dietary change.
Recognize and reinforce a fragile action-stage behavior change using patient-centered counseling, while gently correcting overgeneralized beliefs about carbohydrate quality.
Formulate a nutrition diagnosis and a realistic, budget- and pantry-compatible meal plan for a household of eight that addresses sweet tea/juice intake, late-night snacking, and meal skipping.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Fragile action-stage dietary change in a pregnant woman (BMI 30, prediabetes) with inconsistent prenatal vitamin adherence and food-insecurity-driven eating pattern
differential: Excessive carbohydrate/added sugar intake relative to glucose tolerance in pregnancy with prediabetes
Inadequate micronutrient intake from inconsistent prenatal vitamin use
Food insecurity/under-eating (skipped meals) secondary to household resource allocation
Behavioral risk of relapse from a very recently adopted, unsupported dietary change
Elevated BP (135/88) and lipid pattern (TC 211, LDL 133.3) warranting monitoring but not yet a nutrition diagnosis requiring urgent referral
keyFindings: Fasting glucose 77.3 mg/dL, within normal range
BMI 30 kg/m2 (obese class I); weight +5.3 kg since 2023-06-02 (~3 years, not acute gestational gain)
BP 135/88 mmHg, HR 93 - borderline elevated, flag for OB follow-up not acute action
Diet pattern: budget-driven, starch-heavy, feeds household of 8; recently added oatmeal breakfast and more water (weeks-old change)
Skips own lunch so younger kids eat first; late-night snacking; finishes kids' sweet tea/juice
Uses sales flyers and food pantry near her church to stretch budget
Reports taking prenatal vitamin 'most days'; OB record from 2026-08-21 documents a full week in August 2026 with no vitamin use due to nausea - a mismatch she has not volunteered to this learner
No alcohol/tobacco concerns (ex-smoker, AUDIT-C 1); no known allergies
2023 CBC (hemoglobin 17.3, WBC 4.7, platelets 211.7) predates current pregnancy and is not relevant to current nutrition status
plan: Complete ADIME nutrition assessment: diet history, 24-hr recall or typical day, anthropometrics, relevant labs, psychosocial/food access barriers

Nutrition diagnosis (PES): e.g., 'Inconsistent carbohydrate/meal timing related to household food allocation and limited support as evidenced by self-reported meal skipping and new but fragile dietary changes'
Reinforce and anchor recent wins (oatmeal breakfast, increased water) with specific, low-burden strategies to sustain them through a stressful week
Provide portion- and timing-specific guidance on carbohydrate choices to correct the 'good carbs are always fine' overgeneralization, using her existing knowledge as a base
Address meal skipping: counsel on ensuring she eats a protein/fiber-containing meal at the same time as feeding the kids, not after
Discuss practical budget- and pantry-compatible meal planning for a household of 8 (e.g., building meals around rice/beans/eggs/frozen vegetables, pantry inventory check)
Address sweet tea and finishing kids' juice: suggest realistic substitutions or portion limits rather than elimination
Gently explore prenatal vitamin adherence pattern and taking it with food/snack to reduce nausea; normalize the difficulty without judgment
Flag mismatch between patient self-report and OB documentation for care-team communication (not confrontation) and encourage her to raise it with her OB
Screen briefly for emotional wellbeing related to the prior loss and current pregnancy anxiety; refer to OB/behavioral health if distress is significant
Communicate elevated BP/HR and lipid values to the OB team for their follow-up; this is outside dietetics scope to manage directly
Schedule a focused follow-up visit in 2-4 weeks to reassess adherence and reinforce changes
redFlags: Any report of persistent vomiting/inability to retain fluids or vitamins (hyperemesis) - not currently present but worth monitoring
BP trending higher or new symptoms (headache, visual changes, swelling worsening) suggestive of preeclampsia - refer to OB urgently if it emerges
Expressed thoughts of self-harm or severe depressive symptoms tied to miscarriage anxiety - refer to behavioral health/OB immediately if disclosed
Complete cessation of prenatal vitamin for extended periods without clinical follow-up
educationPoints: Oatmeal and beans are good complex-carbohydrate choices, but portion size and pairing with protein/fat still matter for blood sugar in pregnancy with prediabetes
Skipping her own meals to feed the kids first can worsen fatigue and blood sugar swings and is not necessary even on a tight budget
Small, sustainable swaps (like the ones she's already started) are more durable than big overhauls, especially with low household support
Taking the prenatal vitamin with a small snack rather than on an empty stomach can reduce nausea and support more consistent use
It is safe and expected to tell her OB about gaps in vitamin use; this isn't about being 'in trouble', it helps the team support her better
Food pantry and sales-flyer shopping are valid, resourceful strategies, not something to be ashamed of; there are ways to build balanced meals from what's available there

mismatches.patientClaim: She reports taking her prenatal vitamin most days, describing lapses as occasional forgetfulness when nausea flares on an empty stomach (h21, s15)
mismatches.recordEvidence: OB visit note from 2026-08-21 documents that she reported a full one-week gap with no prenatal vitamin use that same month due to nausea (d2)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported supplement adherence can minimize the true extent of gaps; cross-checking recent documentation helps the clinician gauge actual intake before building a plan, and the gap should be explored gently rather than confronted.

mismatches.patientClaim: She attributes her weight gain mainly to current stress eating and household demands, not framing it as a multi-year trend (h25)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Weight trend shows a +5.3 kg change from 2023-06-02 to the current visit, a gain accumulated over roughly three years rather than acutely (d4)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Distinguishing gradual, multi-year weight change from acute gestational or recent change is essential for accurate nutrition assessment and avoids over- or under-attributing current eating patterns to a single cause.
